title: A man who never went to school invented a whole writing system in 1821
body: Sequoyah, a Cherokee man born around 1770, never went to school and spoke only Cherokee. Around 1809 he began devising a way to write it, and by 1821 he had a **syllabary of 86 symbols**, one for each syllable rather than each sound. His six-year-old daughter Ayokeh was the first to learn it, and she read words back at a demonstration for sceptical leaders. The Cherokee Nation adopted the system in 1825, and by 1830 as many as 90 per cent of Cherokees could read and write their own language.

slides.question: An alphabet spells sounds; Sequoyah’s Cherokee syllabary spells syllables. How many symbols did it need?
slides.explanation: 86, one for each syllable, such as ‘ka’ or ‘tsu’, rather than each sound. One symbol was dropped when the syllabary was adapted for printing in 1828, so modern Cherokee uses 85.

slides.alt: Three rows compare writing systems: an alphabet with one sign per sound and 26 letters; a syllabary with one sign per syllable and 85 symbols; and logographic writing with one sign per word and thousands of characters.
slides.caption: An alphabet spells sounds, a syllabary spells syllables, so Cherokee gets by with about 85 signs.

slides.label: of Cherokees could read their own language by 1830, five years after adoption
slides.text: Within a quarter-century, literacy in the Cherokee Nation was close to 100 per cent.

slides.heading: By 1830, as many as 90 in 100 Cherokees could read and write their own language
slides.note: Five years after the Cherokee Nation adopted the syllabary, and nine after Sequoyah finished it.

The Cherokee Nation officially adopts it
The Cherokee Phoenix, a bilingual newspaper, is founded

slides.heading: Syllables, not letters
slides.text: Each symbol stands for a whole syllable, such as ‘ka’ or ‘tsu’, so a word needs fewer signs than in an alphabet. That may be one reason the system could be learned so fast, and why a people with no tradition of writing became literate within a generation.

slides.heading: Earliest first
items: Sequoyah starts work on the system
slides.explanation: He began around 1809, finished in 1821, the Nation adopted it in 1825, and the newspaper followed in 1828.
